items.zh: 六妙門 · 與觀相應、修還
parent: The Six Wondrous Gates: Cultivation and Realization

zh: 二、與觀相應者，如是觀時，覺息入出，遍諸毛孔，心眼開明，徹見內三十六物及諸蟲戶內外不淨，眾苦逼迫，剎那變易，一切諸法悉無自性，心生悲喜，無所依倚，得四念處，破四顛倒，是名與觀相應。觀解既發，心緣觀境，分別破析，覺念流動，非真實道，爾時應當捨觀修還。
en: Second, correspondence with contemplation: contemplating in this way, one becomes aware of the breath going out and coming in, pervading every pore of the body, the mind's own eye opening into clarity, seeing through entirely to the thirty-six substances within and the various parasites there, impure both within and without, every kind of suffering pressing in, changing moment to moment, every dharma whatsoever without any nature of its own — the mind gives rise to both sorrow and joy, with nothing at all to depend upon or lean against, attaining the four foundations of mindfulness, breaking through the four inversions — this is named correspondence with contemplation. Once this contemplative understanding has arisen, the mind takes the very object of contemplation itself as its object, discriminating and analyzing it further — its perceiving and thinking still in flux, this is not yet the true path — at this point, one should relinquish contemplation and cultivate returning instead.

zh: 還亦有二：一者、修習還；二者、與還相應。一、修習還者，既知觀從心發，若隨析境，此則不會本源，應當返觀此心者從何而生：為從觀心生，為從非觀心生？若從觀心生，則先已有觀，今實不爾。所以者何？數、隨、止等三法之中，未有觀故。若非觀心生，不觀心為滅生，為不滅生？若不滅生，即二心並；若是滅法已謝，不能生現在；若言亦滅亦不滅生，乃至非滅非不滅生，皆不可得。當知觀心本自不生，不生故不有，不有故即空，空無觀心。若無觀心，豈有觀境？境智雙忘，還源之要，是名修還。
en: Returning, too, is of two kinds: cultivating returning; and correspondence with returning.

First, cultivating returning: already knowing that contemplation arises from the mind itself, if one simply follows along analyzing its object, this fails to meet the original source directly — one should instead turn the contemplation back upon this very mind, asking from what it itself arises: does it arise from a contemplating mind, or from a non-contemplating mind? If it arises from a contemplating mind, then contemplation would already have to be present beforehand — but this is, in truth, not so at all. Why is this? Because, within the three prior dharmas of counting, following, and stilling, no contemplation is yet present. If it arises instead from a non-contemplating mind, does this non-contemplating mind arise through cessation, or without cessation? If it arises without cessation, then two minds would exist together at once; if it is a ceased dharma that has already passed away, it cannot give rise to anything present now; and if it is said to arise through both cessation and non-cessation together, or, further still, through neither cessation nor non-cessation, none of these can be found to hold up either. One should know, then, that the contemplating mind is, in itself, originally unarisen — and, being unarisen, it does not exist; and, not existing, it is thus empty — and this very emptiness has no contemplating mind present within it at all. If there is no contemplating mind, how, then, could there be any object of contemplation? Object and wisdom both forgotten together — this is the very essential of returning to the source — this is named cultivating returning.

zh: 二、與還相應者，心慧開發，不加功力，任運自能破析，返本還源，是名與還相應。既相應已，行者當知，若離境智，欲歸無境智，不離境智，縛心隨二邊故，爾時當捨還。
en: Second, correspondence with returning: mind and wisdom now open forth, without any further application of effort, spontaneously able of themselves to analyze and break through, turning back to the very root and returning to the source — this is named correspondence with returning. Once this correspondence has arisen, the practitioner should know that, wishing to leave both object and wisdom behind and return to a state with neither object nor wisdom at all, while still not yet actually free of object and wisdom, the mind remains bound, following one or the other of these two extremes — at this point, one should relinquish returning as well.

The tetralemma against a findable "contemplating mind" (does it arise from a contemplating mind or a non-contemplating mind — and, if the latter, through that mind's cessation, its non-cessation, both, or neither?) is the same four-alternative analysis this treatise has run repeatedly since fascicle 1 — against "contaminated dharma," against "offense," against "karma" — now turned reflexively on contemplation itself, the very faculty doing the analyzing in every prior instance. This is a genuinely elegant closing of the loop: having used contemplative analysis to dissolve object after object, returning finally asks whether the analyzing mind itself can survive its own method, and finds that it cannot — "object and wisdom both forgotten together."

zh: 安心淨道亦有二：一者、修淨；二者、與淨相應。一、修淨者，知色淨故，不起妄想分別，受、想、行、識亦復如是。息妄想垢，息分別垢，息取我垢，是名修淨。舉要言之，若能心如本淨，名為修淨；亦不得能所修及淨、不淨，是名修淨。二、與淨相應者，作是修時，豁然心慧相應，無礙方便，任運開發，三昧正受，心無依倚。
en: Settling the mind upon the path of purity is likewise of two kinds: cultivating purity; and correspondence with purity.

First, cultivating purity: knowing that form is itself pure, one no longer gives rise to deluded thought or discrimination regarding it — and the same holds for sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness as well. Bringing to rest the defilement of deluded thought, the defilement of discrimination, and the defilement of grasping at a self — this is named cultivating purity. Stated in essence: if the mind is able to be exactly as originally pure, this is named cultivating purity; and, finding no subject that cultivates and no object cultivated, no purity and no impurity either, this too is named cultivating purity.

Second, correspondence with purity: practicing in this way, the mind and wisdom suddenly correspond with one another, unobstructed and skillful, opening forth spontaneously of their own accord, the samādhi properly received, the mind with nothing at all to depend upon or lean against.

zh: 證淨亦有二：一者、相似證，五方便相似無漏慧發；二者、真實證，苦法忍乃至第九無礙道等三乘真無漏慧發也。三界垢盡，故名證淨。
en: Realizing purity is likewise of two kinds: approximate realization, where a wisdom that only resembles the uncontaminated is brought forth through the five expedient means; and true realization, where the true, uncontaminated wisdom of the three vehicles is brought forth, from the patient acceptance of the truth of suffering all the way through the ninth unobstructed path. The defilement of the three realms entirely exhausted — this is named realizing purity.

items.en: The Six Wondrous Gates Are the Mahāyāna Itself
parent: The Six Wondrous Gates: Cultivation and Realization

zh: 復次，觀眾生空，故名為觀；觀實法空，故名為還；觀平等空，故名為淨。復次，空三昧相應，故名為觀；無相三昧相應，故名為還；無作三昧相應，故名為淨。復次，一切外觀名為觀，一切內觀名為還，一切非內非外觀名為淨。故先尼梵志言：「非內觀故，得是智慧；非外觀故，得是智慧；亦不無觀故，得是智慧。」復次，菩薩從假入空觀，故名為觀；從空入假觀，故名為還；空假一心觀，故名為淨。若能如是修者，當知六妙門即是摩訶衍。
en: Furthermore: contemplating the emptiness of sentient beings is named contemplating; contemplating the emptiness of real dharmas is named returning; and contemplating the emptiness of equality itself is named purifying.

Furthermore: correspondence with the samādhi of emptiness is named contemplating; correspondence with the samādhi of signlessness is named returning; and correspondence with the samādhi of wishlessness is named purifying.

Furthermore: every outward contemplation is named contemplating; every inward contemplation is named returning; and every contemplation that is neither inward nor outward is named purifying. Hence the wandering ascetic Senika says: "Not through inward contemplation is this wisdom attained; not through outward contemplation is this wisdom attained; and yet not without any contemplation at all is this wisdom attained either."

Furthermore: the bodhisattva's contemplation proceeding from the provisional into emptiness is named contemplating; the contemplation proceeding from emptiness back into the provisional is named returning; and the single-minded contemplation of emptiness and the provisional together is named purifying. If one is able to cultivate in this way, one should know that the six wondrous gates are themselves precisely the Mahāyāna.

zh: 復次，三世諸佛入道之初，先以六妙門為本，如釋迦初詣道樹，即內思安般：一、數；二、隨；三、止；四、觀；五、還；六、淨。遊止三四，出生十二，因此證一切法門，降魔成道。當知菩薩善入六妙門，即能具一切佛法，故六妙門即是菩薩摩訶衍。今欲更論餘事，故略說不具足也。
en: Furthermore: at the very outset of entering the path, the buddhas of the three periods of time all take the six wondrous gates as their own foundation — just as, when Śākyamuni first arrived beneath the bodhi tree, he reflected inwardly on mindfulness of the breath: counting; following; stilling; contemplating; returning; and purifying. Roaming and abiding through the third and fourth dhyānas, twelve are brought forth — and, through this, he realized every dharma-gate whatsoever, subdued Māra, and accomplished the path.

One should know, then, that a bodhisattva who properly enters the six wondrous gates is thereby able to be complete in the whole of the Buddhadharma — hence the six wondrous gates are themselves precisely the bodhisattva's own Mahāyāna. Wishing to discuss further matters still, this is given here only in brief, not in full.

The four successive re-descriptions of contemplating/returning/purifying (as objects of contemplation, as the three samādhi-gates, as inward/outward/neither, and as the bodhisattva's own two-truths movement between emptiness and the provisional) is the treatise's characteristic layering technique taken to its fullest extent — the same three-step structure viewed through four entirely different doctrinal vocabularies, each illuminating a different facet without displacing the others. Senika's own formula ("not inward, not outward, and not without any contemplation either") is a compact restatement of the very tetralemma logic just used against the contemplating mind itself. That the six wondrous gates are explicitly identified as what the Buddha himself used beneath the bodhi tree — the exact same claim fascicle 5 made for ānāpāna generally — confirms these gates are not a separate, lesser technique but the full elaboration of that same original method. This closes the six wondrous gates — given here, as the text itself says, only in brief rather than in full.

items.en: The Sixteen Special Excellences: Their Name

zh: 次釋十六特勝，即開為三意：一、釋名；二、明觀門制立不同；三、明修證。第一、釋名者，所言十六特勝者：一、知息入；二、知息出；三、知息長短；四、知息遍身；五、除諸身行；六、受喜；七、受樂；八、受諸心行；九、心作喜；十、心作攝；十一、心作解脫；十二、觀無常；十三、觀出散；十四、觀欲；十五、觀滅；十六、觀棄捨。所以通名十六特勝者，十六即是數法。特勝者，從因緣得名。
en: Next, explaining the sixteen special excellences: this opens into three parts — explaining the name; clarifying the differing schemes for establishing the contemplation-gates; and clarifying their cultivation and realization.

First, explaining the name: as for what is called the sixteen special excellences, these are: knowing the breath entering; knowing the breath leaving; knowing the breath's length and shortness; knowing the breath pervading the whole body; removing every bodily formation; receiving joy; receiving happiness; receiving every mental formation; the mind making joy; the mind making restraint; the mind making liberation; contemplating impermanence; contemplating dispersal; contemplating [freedom from] desire; contemplating cessation; and contemplating relinquishment. As for why they are named, in general, the sixteen special excellences: "sixteen" is simply the number of dharmas involved. "Special excellence" takes its name from the very causes and conditions behind their teaching.

zh: 如佛未出世時，外道等並已修得四禪、四空，而無對治觀行，故不出生死。如來成道，初為拘隣及舍利弗等利根弟子說四真諦，即得道跡。復為摩訶迦葉、絺那等直聞四諦真理不悟，更說不淨觀法對治，破諸煩惱。因此初明九想、背捨等諸不淨觀禪。爾時修此觀者，得道無量。復有一機眾生，貪欲既薄，若厭惡心重，作不淨觀，即大生厭患，便增惡此身，無漏未發，即顧人自害，此事如律文所明，佛因此告諸比丘捨不淨觀，更修勝法，法名十六特勝，修之可以得道。
en: When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, the non-Buddhist teachers had already attained the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations on their own, but, lacking any antidote-contemplation, they never left birth-and-death behind. When the Tathāgata accomplished the path, he first taught the Four Noble Truths to disciples of sharp faculty such as Kauṇḍinya and Śāriputra, and they attained the fruit of the path at once. He then taught Mahākāśyapa, Kaṭyāyana, and others, who, hearing the true principle of the Four Noble Truths directly, failed to awaken through it — and so he further taught the contemplation of impurity as its antidote, breaking through their afflictions. Through this, the nine contemplations, the liberations, and the other contemplations of impurity were first clarified. At that time, those who cultivated this contemplation attained the path in immeasurable numbers.

There was, however, a further kind of disposition among sentient beings: those whose craving was already slight, but whose disgust and aversion ran deep — practicing the contemplation of impurity, they grew greatly disgusted and troubled, coming to loathe this very body all the more, and, the uncontaminated attainment not yet having arisen, they would hire others to kill them or cause themselves harm. This matter is clarified in the Vinaya texts; the Buddha, because of this, told the monks to set the contemplation of impurity aside, and instead cultivate a more excellent dharma, named the sixteen special excellences — cultivating this, the path could still be attained.

zh: 此十六特勝有定有觀，是中具足諸禪，以喜、樂等法愛養故，則無自害之過，而有實觀觀察，不著諸禪，所以能發無漏。既進退從容，不隨二邊，亦能得道，故名特勝。問：若爾，應在觀禪後說淨禪。何以故？若取教門，即在觀禪之後；若論行法，既勝二邊，亦應在後。答：今明禪定力用淺深之相，非是對緣利物之時。所以者何？背捨、勝處悉是得解之觀，觀力既能轉想轉心，於斷結義強。今此特勝唯是實觀，能見身內三十六物，力用劣弱，不能疾斷結使，功德淺薄，故應前說。
en: These sixteen special excellences possess both concentration and contemplation together, complete, within them, with every dhyāna — and, being nourished by the dharmas of joy, happiness, and the rest, are free of the fault of self-harm; and, possessing true contemplation's own careful observation, they do not cling to any dhyāna, and so are able to bring forth the uncontaminated. Since one may thus proceed with ease, advancing or holding back as needed, following neither of the two extremes, and is nonetheless still able to attain the path through them — hence they are named the "special excellences."

Question: if this is so, then this dharma ought properly to be spoken of after the contemplation-dhyānas, being itself the "pure dhyāna." Why is this? If one follows the order of the teaching's own presentation, it comes after the contemplation-dhyānas; and if one discusses the practice itself, since it surpasses both extremes, it, too, ought properly to come afterward.

Answer: what is clarified here is the shallowness and depth of dhyāna-concentration's own power and function, not the timing of when it is actually taught in response to a given situation to benefit beings. Why is this? The liberations and the stations of mastery are all contemplations of understanding attained — their contemplative power is already able to transform both conception and mind, and so their sense of severing the fetters is strong. These special excellences, by contrast, are simply true contemplation, able only to see the thirty-six substances within the body — their power and function are comparatively weak, unable to quickly sever the fetters, their merit comparatively shallow — hence they are properly spoken of first here.

zh: 復次，若不淨觀散滅骨人，則不能得更觀身毛孔息出入相。若於實觀後轉作九想、背捨等，則具足成就，於義無失。復次《大品經．廣乘品》觀於十六特勝。復次，說九想、背捨等諸觀禪，此為明證，不應生疑也。
en: Furthermore: if the contemplation of impurity has already dissolved the skeleton entirely away, one would no longer be able to go on to contemplate the breath entering and leaving through the body's own pores. If, instead, one proceeds from true contemplation and only afterward turns to the nine contemplations, the liberations, and the rest, then both are fully accomplished, without any loss of sense. Furthermore, the Larger Sūtra's own chapter on the vast vehicle contemplates the sixteen special excellences; and, furthermore, it then speaks of the nine contemplations, the liberations, and the other contemplation-dhyānas — this is clear evidence of the order, and there should be no doubt raised about the matter.

The origin story here gives the sixteen special excellences a genuinely different rationale than anything offered for the contemplation of impurity earlier in the treatise: not a more advanced technique, but a safer one for a specific, dangerous failure mode — practitioners whose craving is already slight but whose self-directed disgust runs so deep that contemplating the body's impurity tips them toward self-harm before the antidote has actually taken hold. That the treatise places these "special excellences" before the very contemplations they were designed to make safer, despite conceding the special excellences are weaker and slower on their own terms, is a clear statement of method: sequencing here follows the shallowness and depth of each method's own power and function — the weaker true contemplation before the stronger contemplations of understanding attained — not the order in which they were taught to benefit beings.

quiz.q: In correspondence with contemplation, what does the practitioner see and attain?
options: the breath through every pore, seeing the thirty-six substances and parasites; sorrow and joy arise; one attains the four foundations of mindfulness and breaks the four inversions
quiz.why: The breath is felt through every pore, the mind's eye sees the thirty-six substances and parasites, sorrow and joy arise, and one attains the four foundations of mindfulness, breaking the four inversions.

quiz.q: Once contemplative understanding has arisen, why relinquish contemplation and cultivate returning?
options: the mind keeps analyzing its object, thought still in flux, not the true path
quiz.why: The mind still takes the object, analyzing it, and the thought is in flux, not the true path; so one turns to returning.

quiz.q: In cultivating returning, how does the practitioner turn back the contemplation?
options: knowing contemplation arises from mind, one asks whether it arises from a contemplating or non-contemplating mind
examine whether external objects are real
quiz.why: Knowing contemplation arises from the mind, and that following the object misses the source, one turns back to ask whether this mind arises from a contemplating or a non-contemplating mind.

quiz.q: Why can the contemplating mind not arise from a contemplating mind?
options: contemplation would already exist beforehand, but none is present in counting, following, and stilling
quiz.why: Contemplation would have to exist beforehand, but in the three prior dharmas, counting, following, and stilling, there is no contemplation yet.

quiz.q: If the contemplating mind arose from a non-contemplating mind without its ceasing, what fault follows?
options: it could not produce the present
quiz.why: Without cessation, two minds would coexist; if it had already ceased, it could not produce the present, which is option B's fault.

quiz.q: What conclusion does the investigation of returning reach?
options: the contemplating mind is unarisen, hence nonexistent and empty; without it there is no object, and object and wisdom are both forgotten
it arises from a non-contemplating mind
the object is real, the mind unreal
quiz.why: The contemplating mind is originally unarisen, so nonexistent and empty; with no contemplating mind there is no object, and object and wisdom are both forgotten, the essential of returning to the source.

quiz.q: After corresponding with returning, why relinquish returning as well?
options: it falls back to the desire realm
wishing to leave object and wisdom for their absence, one is still bound, following one of two extremes
quiz.why: Wishing to leave object and wisdom for a state without them, one is not yet free of them and the mind is bound to an extreme; so one relinquishes returning and moves to purity.

quiz.q: Cultivating purity brings which three defilements to rest?
options: deluded thought, discrimination, grasping at self
quiz.why: Knowing form and the other aggregates to be pure, one stills the defilements of deluded thought, discrimination, and grasping at a self.

quiz.q: Stated in essence, what is cultivating purity?
options: severing views in the three realms
the mind as originally pure, finding no cultivator or cultivated, no purity or impurity
quiz.why: If the mind is as originally pure, that is cultivating purity; and finding no subject or object of cultivation, no purity or impurity, is also cultivating purity.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of realizing purity?
options: approximate: approximate uncontaminated wisdom through the five expedients; true: true uncontaminated wisdom from patient acceptance of suffering to the ninth unobstructed path
quiz.why: Approximate realization brings forth approximate uncontaminated wisdom through the five expedients; true realization brings forth the true uncontaminated wisdom of the three vehicles.

quiz.q: Why is it called "realizing purity"?
options: the defilement of the three realms is exhausted
quiz.why: The defilement of the three realms entirely exhausted, it is named realizing purity.

quiz.q: What is correspondence with purity?
options: mind and wisdom suddenly correspond, unobstructed means opening of themselves, samādhi properly received, the mind without support
quiz.why: Mind and wisdom suddenly correspond; unobstructed skillful means open of themselves; samādhi is properly received, the mind leaning on nothing.

quiz.q: Matching three kinds of emptiness to contemplating, returning, and purifying, which is correct?
options: emptiness of beings: contemplating; of real dharmas: returning; of equality: purifying
quiz.why: Contemplating the emptiness of beings is contemplating; that of real dharmas is returning; that of equality is purifying.

quiz.q: Matching the three samādhis to contemplating, returning, and purifying, which is correct?
options: emptiness: contemplating; signlessness: returning; wishlessness: purifying
quiz.why: Correspondence with the samādhi of emptiness is contemplating, with signlessness returning, with wishlessness purifying.

quiz.q: When matching inward and outward contemplation to the three gates, whose words are cited?
quiz.why: Outward contemplation is contemplating, inward is returning, neither is purifying, supported by the words of the wandering ascetic Senika. Subhadra appears at the end of the special excellences.

quiz.q: Matching the bodhisattva's three contemplations to the three gates, which is correct?
options: from provisional to emptiness: contemplating; from emptiness to provisional: returning; both in one mind: purifying
quiz.why: From the provisional into emptiness is contemplating, from emptiness into the provisional is returning, and emptiness and the provisional in one mind is purifying; so practiced, the six gates are the Mahāyāna.

quiz.q: What does the account of Śākyamuni at the bodhi tree illustrate?
options: all buddhas begin with the six gates; Śākyamuni reflected on the six breath methods and through them realized every gate, subdued Māra, and attained the path
he first practiced the immeasurable minds
quiz.why: The buddhas of the three times all begin from the six gates; Śākyamuni reflected on mindfulness of the breath beneath the bodhi tree and through it realized every gate and subdued Māra.

quiz.q: What are the thirteenth through sixteenth special excellences?
options: contemplating dispersal, freedom from desire, cessation, relinquishment
joy, happiness, mental formations, making joy
quiz.why: The last four are contemplating dispersal, desire (freedom from desire), cessation, and relinquishment; the twelfth is impermanence.

quiz.q: How is the name "sixteen special excellences" explained?
options: sixteen is the number; "special excellence" takes its name from the circumstances of its teaching
quiz.why: "Sixteen" is simply the number of dharmas; "special excellence" is named from the causes and conditions of its teaching, explained next.

quiz.q: Why did the Buddha teach Mahākāśyapa and others the contemplation of impurity?
options: hearing the Four Truths directly they did not awaken, so he taught impurity as an antidote
quiz.why: Hearing the true principle of the Four Truths directly, they failed to awaken, so the Buddha taught the contemplation of impurity as an antidote. Sharp disciples like Kauṇḍinya awakened on the truths alone.

quiz.q: What makes the sixteen "special excellences"?
options: concentration and contemplation together; joy and happiness prevent self-harm; true contemplation prevents clinging; balanced, following neither extreme
quiz.why: It has both concentration and contemplation; nourished by joy and happiness, it avoids self-harm; with true contemplation it does not cling; balanced between extremes, it still attains the path. It is weaker at severing fetters, so B is wrong.

quiz.q: An objector says the special excellences should come after the contemplation-dhyānas. On what basis does the text answer?
options: the chronology of the Buddha's teaching
the depth of dhyāna's power and function, not the timing of teaching to benefit beings
quiz.why: The order follows the depth of dhyāna's power and function, not when it was taught; the special excellences are shallower, so they come first.

quiz.q: How does the power of the liberations and stations of mastery compare with the special excellences?
options: the liberations are understanding attained, transforming conception and mind, strong in severing fetters; the excellences are only true contemplation, weaker
quiz.why: The liberations and stations of mastery, as contemplations of understanding attained, transform conception and mind and sever fetters strongly; the special excellences, only true contemplation, are weaker and come first.

quiz.q: What problem arises if impurity contemplation dissolves the skeleton first?
options: one can no longer contemplate the breath entering and leaving through the pores
quiz.why: If impurity contemplation has dissolved the skeleton, the breath through the pores can no longer be contemplated; doing true contemplation first and then the nine contemplations loses nothing.

quiz.q: Which sūtra chapter is cited as discussing the sixteen special excellences?
options: the Larger Sūtra, chapter on the vast vehicle
quiz.why: The Larger Sūtra's chapter on the vast vehicle discusses the sixteen excellences, and §12 cites it again for the word "knowing."

quiz.q: To whom did the Tathāgata first teach the Four Noble Truths, who attained the path at once?
options: sharp disciples such as Kauṇḍinya and Śāriputra
quiz.why: The Buddha first taught Kauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, and other sharp disciples, who attained the path at once; Mahākāśyapa and others needed the impurity contemplation.
